hints: Remember what an element actually is, a sample containing only one type of atom.
Think of familiar elements like $O_2$, diamond, iron metal and argon gas, and what holds their particles together.
Ask yourself which bonding type needs two very different atoms, one to give electrons and one to take them, and whether that can happen with only one type of atom.
walkthrough:
**Recall what an element means**

An element contains only one type of atom. So any bonding inside it must work between identical atoms with identical electronegativity.

Rule to remember:
$$\text{element = one type of atom only}$$

**Check the bonding we do see in elements**

Covalent bonding is in $O_2$, $Cl_2$ and diamond ($C$). Metallic bonding is in $Fe$, $Na$ and $Cu$. Van der Waals forces are between $Ar$ atoms and between $I_2$ molecules.

**Spot why ionic is impossible**

Ionic bonding needs electron transfer from a low electronegativity atom to a high electronegativity atom to make $+$ and $-$ ions. Identical atoms cannot do this, so an element can never be ionic.

options.A: Covalent bonding is very common in elements. Examples are $O_2$, $H_2$, $Cl_2$, diamond and graphite, all held together by shared pairs of electrons between identical atoms.
options.B: Ionic bonding is never found in elements. It requires a cation and an anion formed by electron transfer between atoms of very different electronegativity, typically a metal and a non-metal, so it needs at least two different elements.
options.C: Metallic bonding is the characteristic bonding of metallic elements. Metals like sodium, iron and copper consist of positive ions in a sea of delocalised electrons.
options.D: Van der Waals forces are found between the atoms or molecules of many non-metal elements. Examples are between argon atoms in solid argon and between $I_2$ molecules in solid iodine.
